vignette:
Tane is a 54-year-old man who served for 27 years as a combat pilot in the New Zealand Defence Force. Over our first several sessions, he has described the accident with a careful, almost clinical precision, as if he were still writing a report. That day, three years ago, he was piloting a P-3K2 Orion on a low-level maritime patrol over the Southern Alps. The weather was marginal-low cloud and turbulence. As he banked through a narrow valley, a sudden downdraft slammed the aircraft toward the ridgeline. He pulled hard on the yoke, but the starboard wingtip clipped the tops of a stand of rimu trees. The aircraft yawed violently, the stall warning screamed, and then everything went silent. He ejected moments before the fuselage disintegrated against the rock face. The canopy shattered, and a piece of Perspex sliced into his flight helmet. He woke three days later in Christchurch Hospital with a fractured skull and a cervical spine strain. He was the only survivor.

Since then, Tane has not flown. Not once. He was medically grounded and now works as a logistics coordinator at the same base, a job he describes as "filing paper and watching the sky." He cannot walk past the hangar where his old Orion sits mothballed. On his first day back, he had a panic attack in the car park-sweating, tunnel vision, his heart pounding as if he were still in the ejection seat. Now he parks a block away and enters through a side door. He avoids the tarmac entirely. Even the sound of a C-130 warming up on the runway sends him into a cold sweat.

At home, his wife Maria notices changes she calls "a second person living inside him." He no longer joins her for their Saturday morning walks along the beach, because the distant roar of military jets from the base always seems to find him. He's irritable with her over small things-a dish left in the sink, the volume of the television. At night, he wakes with violent start-ups, convinced he's still falling. On the worst nights, he hears the stall warning tone vibrating in his skull. He has stayed on the couch for the last eight months because Maria's warmth triggers a flash of the cockpit heat just before impact. He tells me he feels "disconnected from everything," like he is watching his life through a dirty window. He cannot remember what it felt like to be excited about anything-not his grandson's birth, not the All Blacks winning the World Cup, not even the prospect of retirement next year.

Driving has become a nightmare. He avoids the coastal road that curves around the hills above the base, because the sight of the same cloud formations that day sends his mind spiraling into vivid replays. He checks his rearview mirror obsessively, expecting to see the mountain rushing toward him. Loud, unexpected sounds-a car backfiring, a door slamming-make him drop to a crouch, his hands covering his head. He once yelled at a bagpiper at a funeral because the drone reminded him of the engine spooling down.

Tane has difficulty trusting his own body. He still walks with a slight limp from a knee injury sustained on ejection, but he refuses physical therapy because the examination table reminds him of the hospital bed where he first learned the co-pilot did not survive. He avoids going to the doctor altogether. He no longer drinks alcohol, which he used to enjoy, because even one beer "loosens the walls" and the memories flood in. He has not had a truly restful night's sleep since the accident.

He tells me he feels like the person who ejected from that aircraft is someone else-a younger man who believed in his own invincibility. The man sitting across from me now is cautious, isolated, and always scanning the horizon for something that might fall out of the sky. He says he has never spoken about these things before, not even to Maria.
